children.html: The Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale: Initial examination of its factor structure and correlates among Brazilian adults
Viren Swami a,b,∗, Angela Nogueira Neves Betanho Campanac, Lucilene Ferreirac, Seishin Barrett a, Amy Sunshine Harris a, Maria da Consolac¸ ão Gomes Cunha Fernandes Tavares c
• a Department of Psychology, University of Westminster, London, UK
• b Department of Psychology, HELP University College, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
• c School of Physical Education, University of Campinas, Campinas, Brazil
Article history: Received 14 October 2010 Received in revised form 7 January 2011 Accepted 7 January 2011
Keywords: Cosmetic surgery Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale Scale translation Brazil

The present study conducted a preliminary examination of the psychometric properties of a recently developed Portuguese translation of the Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale (ACSS; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005). A total of 311 Brazilian adults completed the ACSS along with Portuguese translations of measures of actual–ideal body weight discrepancy, body appreciation, sociocultural attitudes toward appearance, and demographics. Results showed that the Portuguese ACSS reduced to a threefactor solution consisting of the Intrapersonal, Social, and Consider factors uncovered in the original work using the ACSS. Moreover, there were only small sex differences on these subscales. In addition, the Portuguese ACSS showed a good pattern of convergent validity. The availability of the Portuguese ACSS is expected to stimulate more in-depth, quantitative research on attitudes toward cosmetic surgery within the Brazilian context.

In the past decade, body image scholars have noted a dramatic increase in the number of cosmetic surgery procedures performed in North America and Europe (e.g., Dutta, 2008; Sarwer, Crerand, & Gibbons, 2007; Sarwer & Magee, 2006). For instance, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons (2010) reported that 12.5 million elective cosmetic procedures were performed in the United States in 2009, representing a 69% increase since 2000. With women accounting for the vast majority of cosmetic surgery patients (91% in the United States in 2009; American Society of Plastic Surgeons, 2010), feminist scholars have sought to understand cosmetic surgery as an expression and reproduction of patriarchal gender relations, such that women in the West are subject to beauty ideals to a much greater degree than men (e.g., Jeffreys, 2005).

Bordo (2003) has likewise drawn similarities between cosmetic surgery and fashion accessorising, highlighting the extent to which consumers can 'choose' to enhance their physical appearance through elective procedures. Indeed, within the body image

literature, the decision to have cosmetic surgery is typically viewed as an expression of agency regarding a person's own body and, largely based on this perspective, researchers have attempted to identify factors that predict consideration or acceptance of cosmetic surgery. At a broad level, for example, Sarwer et al. (2007) and Sarwer and Crerand (2004) have discussed the normalisation of appearance-enhancing behaviours, positivemedia coverage, higher disposable income among consumers, and the lower cost of surgery as factors that have increased the popularity of cosmetic surgery among Western populations.

At a more proximate level, scholarly attention has focused on the demographic, psychosocial, and individual difference factors that are associated with consideration of cosmetic surgery. In terms of demographic variables, for example, it has been consistently reported that women are more likely to consider having cosmetic surgery than men (e.g., Brown, Furnham, Glanville, & Swami, 2007; Swami, Arteche, et al., 2008; Swami, Chamorro-Premuzic, Bridges, & Furnham, 2009), mirroring actual rates. Other work has reported that Caucasian women are more accepting of cosmetic surgery than African Caribbeans and South Asians, even after controlling for body image, self-esteem, and weight status (Swami, Campana, & Coles, in press). Finally, a higher body mass index (BMI) has been reliably associated with greater acceptance of cosmetic surgery among women (e.g., Markey & Markey, 2009; Swami, 2009a; Swami, Campana, et al., in press).

In terms of psychosocial variables, the available research has shown that consideration of cosmetic surgery is positively associated with greater exposure to media messages about cosmetic surgery (Crockett, Pruzinsky, & Persing, 2007; Delinsky, 2005; Sperry, Thompson, Sarwer, & Cash, 2009; Swami, Arteche, et al., 2008) and knowing others who have had cosmetic surgery (Brown et al., 2007; Delinsky, 2005; Swami, Arteche, et al., 2008). Similarly, greater appearance-related teasing (Markey & Markey, 2009), romantic relationship satisfaction (Swami & Mammadova, 2011), and paternal attitudes toward appearance (Henderson-King & Brooks, 2009) have all also been associated with consideration of cosmetic surgery. To date, however, the majority of research on consideration or acceptance of cosmetic surgery has focused on individual psychological variables.

The most developed of this research has shown significant and reliable associations between consideration of cosmetic surgery and more negative body image (Crerand, Franklin, & Sarwer, 2006; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005; Markey & Markey, 2009; Sarwer, Wadden, Pertschuk, & Whitaker, 1998; Slevec & Tiggemann, 2010; Swami, 2009a, 2010; Swami, Campana, et al., in press). Other work has reported that greater consideration of cosmetic surgery is correlated with higher investment in appearance (Delinsky, 2005; Sarwer, LaRossa, Bartlett, Low, Bucky, & Whitaker, 2003; Sarwer et al., 2005), greater social conformity (Swami, Chamorro-Premuzic, et al., 2009), higher appearancebased rejection sensitivity (Park, Calogero, Harwin, & DiRaddo, 2009), greater internalisation of media messages about appearance (Henderson-King & Brooks, 2009; Markey & Markey, 2009; Swami, 2009a), greater celebrity worship (Swami, Taylor, & Carvalho, 2009), greater materialist values (Henderson-King & Brooks, 2009), and lower self-esteem (Swami, Campana, et al., in press).

Although this research appears to be thriving, an important limitation is the fact that, almost without exception, samples in the above studies have been drawn from relatively affluent, Western populations. Indeed, some scholars have noted the lack of studies on attitudes toward cosmetic surgery in non-Western and developing nations (e.g., Swami, 2010). This is important because there may be cross-cultural differences in attitudes toward cosmetic surgery or reasons for considering cosmetic surgery. For example, crosscultural differences in socioeconomic status, the role of women in society, and opportunities to shape mate choice may all affect the legitimacy of appearance-enhancing procedures, as has been discussed in relation to body size ideals (e.g., Swami & Tovée, 2005). More broadly, differences in cultural values between developed societies and rapidly modernising nations may impact upon both the importance of the body aesthetic and the way in which societal standards of appearance are regulated and monitored. Indeed, in the context of Malaysia, Swami (2010) has discussed the way in which cultural values associated with collectivism (as opposed to the individualism of Western societies) may result in social influence and interconnectedness becoming as important as individual decision-making when it comes to attitudes toward cosmetic surgery.

As a contribution to the above literature, therefore, the present study sought to examine acceptance of cosmetic surgery and its correlates among adults in Brazil, the largest national economy in Latin America. Brazil offers a useful site in which to examine attitudes toward cosmetic surgery for several reasons. First, Brazil has the highest number of cosmetic surgery procedures per capita in the world, with only the United States and China exceeding Brazil in the total number of surgeries performed annually (International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, 2010). Second, elective cosmetic surgery is widely available in Brazil, with field scholars such as Edmonds (2007) and Dorneles de Andrade (2010) underscoring the ubiquity of cosmetic studios, clinics, and hospitals, particularly

in Rio de Janeiro. Moreover, some public hospitals in Brazil offer cosmetic surgery procedures at no cost to the patient, whereas a saturated private sector has resulted in extremely low prices (Edmonds, 2007). Third, as noted by Edmonds (2007), the mass media in Brazil have been very positive about cosmetic surgery, viewing the growth of the industry and cosmetic surgery tourism as an indicator of economic health or national pride.

Finally, accounts by anthropologists have identified unique aspects of Brazilian culture and society that possibly result in more positive attitudes toward cosmetic surgery. For instance, both Edmonds (2007) and Goldenberg (2002) have highlighted the high value assigned to the corporeal self by Brazilians and have identified the body itself as a status symbol. Indeed, Edmonds goes further in seeing physical appearance as an essential element in the construction of a national Brazilian identity (uma identidade nacional brasileira). Moreover, Edmonds (2007, pp. 364–365) suggests that Western accounts of cosmetic surgery may be insufficient in Brazil, where a democratic "right to beauty" implies that that the "poor have the right to be beautiful". More specifically, cosmetic surgery:

...taps into the aspirations of people on the margins of the market economy. Beauty practices offer a means to compete in... a neoliberal libidinal economy where anxieties surrounding new markets of work and sexmingle with fantasies of socialmobility, glamour, and modernity (Edmonds, 2007, p. 366).

In this view, the cult of the body in Brazil has been paralleled by the attachment of extreme importance to a "well-shaped body" (Goldenberg, 2002, p. 29), a weakening of moral restrictions on body-altering practices, and a normalisation of body modification strategies aimed at social ascent (Dorneles de Andrade, 2010; Edmonds, 2007). Cosmetic surgery, then, serves to express class distinctions, allowing the poor to challenge upper class hegemony on 'beauty' while simultaneously bringing the body into capitalist production and reproduction. While it is important to note discursive challenges to this cult of the body (e.g., see Dorneles de Andrade, 2010), it nevertheless appears to be the case that cosmetic surgery in Brazil has become a mass phenomenon with important implications for society and individuals.

The extant work on attitudes toward cosmetic surgery in Brazil has typically utilised a qualitative framework at the expense of more focused quantitative research. A first aim of the present study, therefore, was to examine attitudes toward cosmetic surgery from a quantitative perspective. Specifically, we examined the factor structure of the most widely used scale for the measurement of attitudes toward cosmetic surgery, namely the Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale (ACSS; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005). This is an important first step, as the factor structure of the ACSS may not be cross-culturally invariant, having been shown to consist of three subscales among Western samples (e.g., Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005) and two subscales among one non-Western sample (Swami, 2010).

An additional aim of the present study was to examine correlates of acceptance of cosmetic surgery in the Brazilian context. Specifically, we examined the associations between acceptance of cosmetic surgery and known predictors among Western samples, namely actual–ideal weight discrepancy (women only), body appreciation, internalisation of media messages about appearance, and weight status (operationalised as self-reported BMI). Given that scales for the first three of these factors have not, to our knowledge, been translated into Portuguese, a secondary aim of the present study was to prepare translations of the Photographic Figure Rating Scale (Swami, Salem, Furnham, & Tovée, 2008b), the Body Appreciation Scale (Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005), and the Sociocultural Attitude Toward Appearance Questionnaire-3 (Thompson, van den Berg, Roehrig, Guarda, & Heinberg, 2004) for use in the present study.

The participants of this study consisted of 195 women and 116 men recruited from among students and staff at two universities in the state of São Paulo. Participants had a mean age of 29.32 years (SD = 11.02) and a mean self-reported BMI of 23.27 kg/m2. The majority of participants described themselves asWhite (79.4%), 11.0% as Brown (Multiracial), and 6.1% as Black, while 3.5% chose not to declare their ethnicity. In terms of educational qualifications, 2.2% had no formal education, 5.5% had completed primary education, 40.2% had completed secondary education, 19.6% had an undergraduate degree, and 31.5% had a further degree or specialist diploma.
Acceptance of Cosmetic Surgery Scale (ACSS; Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005)

The 15-item ACSS is the most widely used scale for the measurement of attitudes toward cosmetic surgery. Among Western samples, it has been reported to reduce into three subscales, namely Intrapersonal (5 items measuring attitudes related to the selforiented benefits of cosmetic surgery), Social (5 items measuring social motivations for having cosmetic surgery), and Consider (5 items measuring the likelihood that a participant would consider having cosmetic surgery). Among a Malaysian sample, however, Swami (2010) reported that the ACSS was best reduced to two factors, consisting of the Consider subscale and an amalgamation of the Intrapersonal and Social subscales. Items in the ACSS are rated on a 7-point scale (1 = Strongly disagree, 7= Strongly agree) and it has been shown to have high internal consistency, good test–retest reliability after three weeks, and good convergent and divergent reliability amongWestern samples (Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005).
Photographic Figure Rating Scale (PFRS; Swami, Salem, et al., 2008)

The PFRS was used to measure actual–ideal weight discrepancy and consists of 10 greyscale photographic images of real women representing the full range of BMI categories. Only female participants were asked to complete the scale by rating the figure that most closely matched their own body and the figure that they would most like to possess (1 = Figure with the lowest BMI, 10 = Figure with the highest BMI). A measure of ideal–actual weight discrepancy was computed as the difference between unsigned (absolute) current and ideal ratings. Previous work has shown that the PFRS retains cross-cultural validity (Swami, Henderson, Custance, & Tovée, in press) and that scores derived from the scale have high construct validity, good test–retest reliability after three weeks, and good construct validity (Swami, Salem, et al., 2008; Swami, Taylor, & Carvalho, in press).
Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos et al., 2005)

The BAS is a 13-item measure of positive body image, in which items are rated on a 5-point scale (1 = Never, 5= Always). Among Western samples, the BAS has been shown to have a one-dimensional structure, but work with a non-Western sample has suggested that it may consist of two subscales measuring General body appreciation and Body image investment (Swami & Chamorro-Premuzic, 2008). Among Western samples, the BAS has been shown to have good discriminant, construct, and incremental
validities (Avalos et al., 2005; Swami, Stieger, Haubner, & Voracek, 2008).
Sociocultural Attitudes Toward Appearance Questionnaire-3 (SATAQ-3; Thompson et al., 2004)

The SATAQ-3 is a 30-item scale measuring the multidimensional impact of sociocultural influences on body image. Items are rated on a 5-point scale (1 = Strongly disagree,5= Strongly agree) and, among Western samples, the scale has been shown to consist of four factors measuring the degree to which various media are considered an important source of information about being attractive (Information), feeling pressured by various media to strive for cultural ideals of beauty (Pressure), endorsement and acceptance of media messages touting unrealistic ideals for female beauty and the striving toward these ideals (Internalisation-General), and endorsement and acceptance of an athletic and toned body ideal (Internalisation-Athlete). However, cross-cultural work with the scale has suggested that it may reduce to three, rather than four, subscales namely an amalgamation of Pressure and General Internalisation, Information, and Internalisation-Athlete (Swami, 2009b). Among Western samples, the scale has been shown to be internally reliable and to have good discriminant and convergent validities (Thompson et al., 2004).

Participants provided their demographic details, consisting of sex, age, ethnicity, highest educational qualification, and selfreported height and weight. The latter two variables were used to calculate participants' BMI as kg/m2.

Portuguese versions of the four scales described above were prepared according to the five-step guideline for the cross-cultural adaptation of health-related measures supported by the Institute forWork and Health (Beaton, Bombardier, Guillemin, & Bosi-Ferraz, 2000). The first step in the adaptation consisted of a translation of the scales from English into Brazilian Portuguese by two independent translators in Brazil who are native speakers of Brazilian Portuguese. The second step consisted of a synthesis of the two forward translations into one Portuguese version, mediated by the two original translators. In a third step, this Portuguese version was back-translated into English by two further independent translators who are native English speakers and naïve to the body image field.

Two independent back-translation versions were produced and, in the fifth step, these were submitted to an expert committee comprising the four translators, a methodologist, a linguist, and two psychologists, all of whom were bilingual in English and Portuguese. The committee used the source scales and the four translations as working tools to evaluate the equivalence of the source and target versions in four areas: semantic equivalence (ensuring meaning and grammatical correctness), idiomatic equivalence (formulating equivalent expressions for colloquialism or idioms), experiential equivalence (ensuring cultural relevance of tasks and examples being used in the test), and conceptual equivalence (ensuring conceptual meaning for the Brazilian population). Through this process, the committee developed pre-final versions of each of the four scales and requested that several items in the BAS and SATAQ-3 be re-written in the affirmative (see Karazsia & Crowther, 2008).

The participants were asked to rate each item in the questionnaire on a 3-point scale for adequacy of translation (1 = Appropriate translation, 2= Moderately appropriate translation; 3= Inappropriate translation, requires modification). If two or more participants rated an item as inappropriately translated and requiring modification, that item was revised by the expert committee (number of items requiring alteration was <5%, mainly the change of items into the affirmative to prevent loss of item equivalency). Through this process, final versions of each scale were prepared in Portuguese for use in the present study.

Prior to conducting this research, ethical approval was obtained from the ethics committee at the relevant university in Brazil. A total of six experimenters recruited participants directly through opportunistic sampling at various campus locations. Participants were invited to take part in a study on body image and completed a consent form prior to participation. All participants completed anonymous, paper-and-pencil versions of the questionnaire at a quiet campus location before returning their questionnaires to the experimenter. All participants were verbally debriefed once they had returned their questionnaires. Participation was on a voluntary basis and participants did not receive any form of remuneration.

The 15 items of the Portuguese ACSS were subjected to an exploratory factor analysis (EFA). The significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity, -2(105) = 2155.12, p < .001, and the size of the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy, KMO = .91, showed that the 15 items had adequate common variance for factor analysis. We, therefore, conducted an EFA using Varimax rotation. The number of factors to be extracted was determined by eigenvalues > 1.0, inspection of the Scree plot (Cattell, 1966), and an extraction criteria of .40 (Kline, 1986). Based on these criteria, three factors emerged with eigenvalues > 1.0 after six iterations, with no major decline between the rotated factors of the solution ( = 3.70, 3.07, and 2.53, with 24.7%, 20.5%, and 16.8% of the variance explained, respectively).

Based on Kline's (1986) criterion, a number of items crossloaded onto two factors and we, therefore, selected item loadings based on the three-factor model initially proposed by Henderson-King and Henderson-King (see Table 1). Cronbach's ˛ for the three

subscales were as follows: Intrapersonal, .82; Social, .81, and Consider, .87. Henderson-King and Henderson-King (2005) also suggest that it is permissible to compute a total acceptance score by taking the mean of all 15 items. In the present study, Cronbach's ˛ for this overall score was .91.

We initially sought to examine whether there were significant sex differences on the subscale scores, computed by taking the mean of items associated with each factor, or on the overall score. An independent sample t-tests showed that there was no significant sex difference on the overall ACSS score (women M = 3.67, SD = 1.27; men M = 3.61, SD = 1.40), t(309) = 0.36, p = .721, d = 0.04. In addition, there were no significant sex differences on the Intrapersonal factor (women M = 4.33, SD = 1.43; men M = 4.51, SD = 1.46), t(309) = 1.08, p = .281, d = 0.12, or on the Social factor (women M = 2.75, SD = 1.41; men M = 2.81, SD = 1.40), t(309) = 0.39, p = .699, d = 0.04. On the other hand, women were significantly more likely to have higher scores on the Consider subscale (women M = 3.93, SD = 1.67; men M = 3.52, SD = 1.86), although the effect size of this difference was small, t(309) = 2.02, p = .045, d = 0.23.

As above, the 13 items of the Portuguese BAS were subjected to an EFA. The significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity, -2(78) = 1610.21, p < .001, and the size of the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy, KMO = .90, both showed that the items of the BAS had adequate common variance for factor analysis. We, therefore, conducted an EFA using Varimax rotation where the number of factors to be extracted was determined based on the same criteria noted above. Based on these criteria, it was possible to extract two factors with eigenvalues > 1.0 after three iterations, with a steep decline between the rotated factors of the solution ( = 5.35 and 1.74, with 41.1% and 13.4% of the variance explained, respectively).

In a previous study with a non-Western sample, Swami and Chamorro-Premuzic (2008) reported that the BAS reduced into two factors, which they named General body appreciation and Body image investment, following the removal of two items (items 7 and 11). The results of the present study appeared to mirror those findings, with the exception that items 7 and 11 loaded onto the General body appreciation factor (see Table 2). As such, we followed the general guidelines reported by Swami and Chamorro-Premuzic (2008) in extracting two factors, the first of which related to General body appreciation and containing ten items. The 30 items of the Portuguese SATAQ-3 were similarly subjected to an EFA using Varimax rotation, as the significance of Bartlett's test of sphericity, \chi^2(78) = 6981.84, p < .001, and the size of the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy, KMO = .93, showed that these items had adequate common variance for factor analysis. Based on the extraction criteria denoted above, we extracted four factors with eigenvalues \lambda > 1.0 after five iterations. There was major decline between the rotated factors of the solution (\lambda = 6.17, 5.85, 4.64, and 3.37, explaining 20.6%, 19.5%, 15.0%, and 11.2% of the variance, respectively). As can be seen in Table 3, none of the items cross-loaded and items were reduced into the four factors originally delineated by Thompson et al. (2004). Cronbach's \alpha for these four factors were as follows: Information, 94; Internalisation–General, .93; Pressures, .91, and Internalisation-Athlete, .88.

We next examined whether there were significant sex differences on any of these subscales. Results of a series of independent sample t-tests showed that there were no significant sex differences on Information (women M = 3.04, SD = 1.11; men M = 2.97, SD = 1.16), t (309) = 0.48, p = .629, d = 0.05, or on Internalisation-Athlete (women M = 2.71, SD = 1.13; men M = 2.49, SD = 1.23), t (309) = 1.61, p = .108, d = 0.18. On the other hand, women had significantly higher scores on Internalisation-General (women M = 2.32, SD = 1.03; men M = 1.97, SD = 1.00), t (309) = 2.83, p = .005, d = 0.32, and Pressures (women M = 2.36, SD = 1.07; men M = 2.08, SD = 1.08), t (309) = 2.19, p = .029, d = 0.24.

As an initial examination of the correlates of acceptance of cosmetic surgery in Brazil, we computed bivariate correlations between the overall ACSS score, General body appreciation, actual-ideal body weight discrepancy (women only, M=1.07, SD=1.15), the four SATAQ-3 subscales, participant age, and BMI, for women and men separately. As can be seen in Table 4, among women, higher acceptance of cosmetic surgery scores were significantly correlated with lower General body appreciation, greater actual-ideal body weight discrepancy, higher scores on all four SATAQ-3 subscales, and higher self-reported BMI. The same pattern of significant correlations was found among men, with the exception of the lack of a significant association between the overall ACSS scores and the Information subscale of the SATAQ-3. These findings suggest that the Portuguese ACSS generally has good convergent validity.

The first aim of the present study was to examine the factor structure of the ACSS among Portuguese-speaking Brazilian adults. Although previous work has suggested that the scale's structure may vary across cultures (Swami, 2010), the present study found that the Portuguese ACSS was best reduced to a three-factor solution similar to the original structure reported by Henderson-King and Henderson-King (2005). Specifically, we found that the Portuguese ACSS consisted of three factors (Social, Intrapersonal, and Consider), each of which had adequate internal consistency (all > .70; Kline, 1986). Moreover, the overall score of the Portuguese ACSS showed very high internal consistency, suggesting that it may be a reliable measure of overall acceptance of cosmetic surgery.

The results of the present study also suggest that the Portuguese ACSS has adequate convergent validity. Specifically, we found that higher acceptance of cosmetic surgery was significantly correlated with lower General body appreciation, greater internalisation of media messages about appearance (all four SATAQ-3 subscales among women, and three of the four subscales among men), and a higher self-reported BMI. Although it should be noted that the strength of these correlations were small to moderate, they nevertheless suggest that the Portuguese ACSS shows a pattern of correlates that is theoretically plausible. In addition, the present results are consistent with previous work showing that acceptance of cosmetic surgery is correlated with body appreciation (e.g., Swami, 2009a, 2010), internalisation of media messages about appearance (Henderson-King & Brooks, 2009; Markey & Markey, 2009; Swami, 2009a), and BMI (e.g., Markey & Markey, 2009; Swami, 2009a; Swami, Campana, et al., in press).
The results of the present study are also notable because they suggest that there are few significant sex differences in acceptance of cosmetic surgery among Brazilian adults. Specifically, we found

no significant sex differences on the overall ACSS score or on the Intrapersonal and Social factors. Moreover, although women were significantly more likely to have higher scores on the Consider subscale of the ACSS, the effect size of this difference was relatively small. These results stand in contrast to previous studies using the ACSS, which have shown that women tend to have significantly higher scores than men on the Interpersonal and Consider subscales of the ACSS (though not on the Social subscale; e.g., Henderson-King & Henderson-King, 2005) and reports that women are more likely to be patients of cosmetic surgery in Brazil (Dorneles de Andrade, 2010)

One possible explanation for this set of findings is that the value assigned to the corporeal self in Brazil is as high among men as it is among women, resulting in more positive attitudes toward body change behaviours. In a similar vein, it is possible that the dramatic increase in cosmetic surgery procedures in Brazil, alongside positive popular discourse of cosmetic surgery (see Edmonds, 2007), has bred more positive attitudes toward surgery among men, even if it has not yet translated into raised numbers of male patients. An alternative explanation for the fact that men and women appear to have similar scores on the Social and Intrapersonal subscales of the ACSS, but are still less likely to consider cosmetic surgery, is that they may be thinking primarily about women having cosmetic surgery when they contemplate the Consider items. That is, they may believe it is acceptable for women to consider having cosmetic surgery, but remain relatively uninterested in having it themselves. Of course, it should also be noted that sampling limitations may have affected our results; our male sample was smaller than our female sample and, in future work, it will be important to re-examine these sex differences with more comparable samples.

Finally, it is also worth considering the results of this study in relation to the SATAQ-3 and BAS. In the first instance, our results showed that the Portuguese SATAQ-3 reduced into the four-factor structure found among Western samples (Thompson et al., 2004) and that each of the four subscales had very good internal consistencies. The Portuguese BAS, on the other hand, was best reduced to a two-factor structure that reflected (though not identically) the structure reported by Swami and Chamorro-Premuzic (2008) for a Malaysian sample. It is possible that the failure to produce a singlefactor structure for the Portuguese BAS may have been a result of translational issues. However, we believe this to be unlikely, given the steps that were taken to ensure that all scales in the present study were translated reliably. It seems more likely that, as was suggested by Swami and Chamorro-Premuzic (2008), the construct of body appreciation as developed by Avalos et al. (2005) may not be cross-culturally stable.

A number of limitations of the present study should be considered. The main shortcoming of our work was the fact that we did not collect information about the socioeconomic status of our participants, who were likely more affluent than the general population in Brazil. Given discourse on cosmetic surgery as a "right" particularly

among poorer section of society and the use of cosmetic surgery to challenge class structures in the Brazilian context (Edmonds, 2007), our failure to collect information about the socioeconomic status of participants means that we are unable to fully engage with this literature. Future studies adopting a quantitative perspective should be encouraged to include measures of socioeconomic status in their design in order to fully account for the processes shaping attitudes toward cosmetic surgery in the Brazilian context.

Second, as we have indicated above, our male sample was smaller than our female sample and this may have influenced our results. Nor can our sample be considered representative of the wider Brazilian population in ways other than socioeconomic status (e.g., ethnicity and educational qualifications), although we attempted to avoid reliance on a fully student sample. Third, we have relied on existing scales that were initially developed for Western samples, and it is possible, despite the care given to our translations, that we have failed to capture attitudes toward cosmetic surgery that may be indigenous to Brazil. In addition to future qualitative work, it may be useful for scholars to begin the task of producing a local variant of the ACSS for use in Brazil.

Future work could also extend the present study by further examining the psychometric properties of the Portuguese ACSS, which we have begun here, and by examining its temporal stability. This may be important because the results of our study suggest that attitudes toward cosmetic surgery in Brazil may be similar to those reported in North America and Britain. Indeed, it was notable that scores on the ACSS were generally high, mirroring scores found in Western settings. To this end, it may also be fruitful to examine responses to the ACSS in different locations within Brazil, such as Rio de Janeiro, where cosmetic surgery may be more popular (see Dorneles de Andrade, 2010). More broadly, we believe it will be important to conduct systematic, cross-cultural examinations of attitudes to cosmetic surgery. The availability of the ACSS in different languages will undoubtedly aid progress in this direction and will afford scholars a clearer picture of the way in which attitudes toward body change behaviours are developing across the world.
